Translingual

Etymology 1

Clipping of English and Latin minimum.

Symbol

min

  1. (mathematics) minimum function

Etymology 2

Clipping of English minute.

Symbol

min

  2. (metrology) minute (accepted for use with the International System of Units)

Etymology 3

Clipping of English and Minangkabau Minangkabau.

Symbol

min

  2. (international standards) ISO 639-2 & ISO 639-3 language code for Minangkabau.

English

Pronunciation

  • IPA(key): /mɪn/
  • Audio (Southern England):(file)
  • Rhymes: -ɪn

Etymology 1

Alternative forms

  • min.

Noun

min (plural mins)

  1. Abbreviation of minute.
  2. (colloquial) Clipping of minute.
    Dinner's ready, darling! – Be there in a min!

Etymology 2

    From Middle English min, from Old English min (“less; small, mean”), from Proto-West Germanic *minni, from Proto-Germanic *minniz (“less”), from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“small, little”). Cognate with Scots min (“less, lesser”), West Frisian min (“small, bad”), Dutch min (“less, small”), Low German minn (“small, low, lean”), German minder (“less”), Icelandic minna (“less”), Latin minus (“less”).

    Alternative forms

    • myn, minne, mynne

    Adjective

    min

    1. (obsolete or UK dialectal, Scotland) Less; smaller; lower.
      • Le Bone Florence (late 1300s)
        The more and the minne
    Derived terms
    • minnock
    Related terms
    • mince

    Etymology 3

    From Middle English min, minne, partly from Old English myne (“mind, intent, desire, love”), from Proto-West Germanic *muni, from Proto-Germanic *muniz (“mind, memory”); and also from Old Norse minni (“memory”), from Proto-Germanic *gaminþiją (“memory, remembrance”); both from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to think”). Related to Icelandic minni (“memory”), German Minne (“love”).

    Noun

    min (plural mins)

    1. (Can we verify(+) this sense?) (obsolete) Memory; remembrance.
      • 1875, Joshiah Gilbet Holland, Sevenoaks:
        […] and faith I've done that same and found me min; […]

    Etymology 4

    From Middle English minnen, mynnen, from Old Norse minna (“to bring to mind”), from minni (“memory”). See above.

    Verb

    min (third-person singular simple present mins, present participle minning, simple past and past participle minned)

    1. (Can we verify(+) this sense?) (transitive, obsolete) to bring to the mind of; remind
    2. (Can we verify(+) this sense?) (transitive, obsolete) to remember
    3. (Can we verify(+) this sense?) (transitive, obsolete) to mention

    Etymology 5

    Alternative forms

    • min.

    Noun

    min (plural mins)

    1. Abbreviation of minimum.
    2. (colloquial) Clipping of minimum.
      Antonym: max
      He's gotta be at least 60, min!
    Derived terms
    • max-min fairness
    • min-entropy
    • min-max
    • min pay
    Translations
    abbreviation for minimum
    • Russian: мин. (ru) (min.)
    • Swedish: min (sv)

    Etymology 6

    Clipping of minoxidil.

    Noun

    min (uncountable)

    1. (informal) minoxidil

    Anagrams

    • INM, NMI, nim

    Asturian

    Alternative forms

    • mi
    • me (Eastern Asturias, accusative)

    Pronunciation

    • IPA(key): /ˈmin/ [ˈmĩŋ]
    • Rhymes: -in
    • Syllabification: min

    Pronoun

    min

    1. me (as the object of a preposition)
    2. (Eastern Asturias) me (dative)
    3. (Western) alternative form of me

    Usage notes

    • In most of Eastern Asturias (Cuenca del Sella) there is a distinction between me (accusative) and mi (dative).
    Garróme en casa ― It caught me at home.
    Garrómilo en casa ― He caught me (for me) it at home

    References

    • “min”, in Diccionariu de la llingua asturiana [Dictionary of the Asturian Language] (in Asturian), 1st edition, Academy of the Asturian Language [Asturian: Academia de la Llingua Asturiana], 2000, →ISBN
    • García Arias, Xosé Lluis (2002–2004), “min”, in Diccionario general de la lengua asturiana [General Dictionary of the Asturian Language] (overall work in Spanish), Editorial Prensa Asturiana, →ISBN

    Etymology

    From Proto-Turkic *bïŋ (“thousand”). Cognate with Old Turkic 𐰉𐰃𐰭 (bïŋ), 𐰋𐰃𐰭 (biŋ), Old Uyghur 𐽹𐽶𐽺𐽷 (mïŋ, “thousand”), Turkish bin (“thousand”), Bashkir мең (meŋ, “thousand”), etc.

    Pronunciation

    • IPA(key): [min]
    • Audio (Baku):(file)

    Numeral

    min

    1. thousand

      Inherited from Proto-Basque *biN.[1] The original meaning could be "bitter", from which the main contemporary meaning of "pain" would be derived.[2]

      3. intimate
      4. (chiefly Northern) strong, intense

        Cornish

          Possibly from Proto-Celtic *maknā, *meknos, from Proto-Indo-European *mak-, *maks- (“bag, belly”). Compare Welsh min.

          Noun

            Etymology 2

            From Middle Dutch min, minne, from Old Dutch minna, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?]; compare Old Frisian minne, Old Saxon minnia, Old High German minna (German Minne).

            1. (poetic) love
              Synonym: liefde
            Usage notes
            • The alternative form minne is used as a deliberate archaism in poetic and historical contexts (as in hoofse minne, which is far more common than hoofse min).

            Indonesian

            Pronunciation

            • (Standard Indonesian) IPA(key): /ˈmin/ [ˈmin]
            • Rhymes: -in
            • Syllabification: min

            Etymology 1

            borrowed from Dutch min, from Middle Dutch min, from Old Dutch min.[1]

            Adjective

            min (comparative lebih min, superlative paling min)

            1. apocopic form of minus

            Etymology 2

            borrowed from Dutch munt, from Middle Dutch mente, minte, from Latin mentha.[1]

            Noun

            min (plural min-min)

            1. mint (any plant in the family Lamiaceae)
            2. mint (the flavouring of the plant)
            3. mint (a green colour, like that of mint)
              min:  
            4. mint (mint-flavored candy, often eaten to sweeten the smell of the breath)

              Middle English

              Etymology 1

              From Old English mīn (“my, mine”), from Proto-Germanic *mīnaz (“my, mine”, pron.) (genitive of *ek (“I”)), from Proto-Indo-European *méynos (“my; mine”).

              Alternative forms

              • mine, minne, myn, myne, mynne, mein, meyne

              Pronunciation

              • IPA(key): /miːn/
              • Rhymes: -iːn

              Determiner

              min (nominative I)

              1. First-person singular genitive determiner: my
              Usage notes

              min is usually used before a vowel and h-, while mi is usually used before a consonant other than h-, much as with Modern English an/a.

              Descendants
              • English: mine (determiner)
              • Scots: mine (determiner)

              Pronoun

              1. First-person singular possessive pronoun: mine, of me

              Norwegian Bokmål

              Etymology 1

              PIE word
              *éǵh₂

              Inherited from Middle Norwegian min, from Old Norse mínn, from Proto-Norse *ᛗᛁᚾᚨᛉ (*minaʀ) (attested in inflected forms), from Proto-Germanic *mīnaz (“my; mine”). The Germanic form continues a pre-Germanic possessive formation *mey-no-s, formed from the oblique stem of Proto-Indo-European *éǵh₂ (“I”) with the adjectival suffix *-nos.

              Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk min, Faroese mín, Icelandic minn, Danish min, Swedish min, German mein and English mine.

              Pronunciation

              • IPA(key): /miːn/, [miːn]
              • (unstressed) IPA(key): /mɪn/, [mɪn]
              • Audio:(file)
              • Rhymes: -iːn
              • Hyphenation: min

              Determiner

              min m (feminine mi, neuter mitt, plural mine)

              1. my; belonging to, associated with, or concerning me.
                Broren min kommer i morgen. ― My brother is coming tomorrow.
                Dette er min beslutning. ― This is my decision.
                • 2021, Lars Saabye Christensen, En tilfeldig nordmann, page 225:
                  de … begynte å gå i min retning
                  They … began to walk in my direction.
                1. (computing) my; designating the current user's personal account, profile, or other individual area.
                  Åpne fanen «Min konto» for å endre passordet. ― Open the “My account” tab to change your password.
                  • 2018 March 26, Sigbjorn, “Hvordan kan jeg se hva jeg har sett på Netflix og slette historikken?”, in Netthjelp‎:
                    Deretter ser du nedover på denne siden til du finner «Min Profil.»
                    Then look further down this page until you find “My Profile.”
              2. (predicative or nominalized) mine; belonging to me.
                Den røde sykkelen er min. ― The red bicycle is mine.
                Du kan låne min. ― You can borrow mine.
                meg og mine — me and my family; me and my loved ones
                Dette betyr mye for meg og mine. ― This means a lot to me and my family.
                • 1908, Henrik Ibsen, chapter IV, in Fru Inger til Østråt‎:
                  tag denne ring, og vær min for Gud og mennesker
                  Take this ring, and be mine before God and humankind.
              3. my; used in affectionate, courteous, or sometimes patronizing forms of address.
                Sov godt, vennen min. ― Sleep well, my dear.
                • 1908, Henrik Ibsen, chapter III, in Fru Inger til Østråt‎:
                  Men tilgiv mig, min ædle jomfru!
                  But forgive me, my noble maiden!
              4. Used before a derogatory description that the speaker applies to themself, often following jeg (“I”).
                Jeg, min tosk, glemte nøklene igjen. ― Fool that I am, I forgot the keys again.
                • 1996, Gunnar Staalesen, De døde har det godt:
                  og jeg, min idiot, jeg trodde hvert ord han sa
                  And I, idiot that I was, believed every word he said.
              5. (colloquial, euphemistic) Used in exclamations with an omitted Gud (“God”), especially du store min, expressing surprise or amazement.
                Du store min, så mye snø det har kommet! ― Goodness me, what a lot of snow has fallen!
                • 1916, Tryggve Andersen, Samlede fortællinger, volume III, page 28:
                  aa du min for et kav
                  Oh my, what a struggle!
              Usage notes
              • The forms agree with the gender and number of the possessed noun, not with the speaker: masculine min, feminine mi, neuter mitt, and plural mine. The same agreement applies when the possessive stands independently.
              • The possessive may precede or follow the noun. A preceding possessive normally accompanies an indefinite noun, as in min sykkel (“my bicycle”); a following possessive normally accompanies a definite noun, as in sykkelen min. Preposed possessives often emphasize ownership, although they also occur without special emphasis in formal or conservative Bokmål.
              • Certain kinship terms may remain indefinite before a following possessive: far min (“my father”), mor mi (“my mother”), and bror min (“my brother”). Forms such as faren min are also accepted.

              Pronoun

              min m (feminine mi, neuter mitt, plural mine)

              1. mine; that which belongs to or is associated with me; used independently, with the possessed noun understood.
                Den røde sykkelen er min. ― The red bicycle is mine.
                Du kan låne min. ― You can borrow mine.
                meg og mine — me and my family; me and my loved ones
                Dette betyr mye for meg og mine. ― This means a lot to me and my family.
                • 1908, Henrik Ibsen, chapter IV, in Fru Inger til Østråt‎:
                  tag denne ring, og vær min for Gud og mennesker
                  Take this ring, and be mine before God and humankind.
              Usage notes
              • The forms agree with the gender and number of the understood noun: masculine min, feminine mi, neuter mitt, and plural mine.
              • Substantivized plural mine can refer to the speaker's family or close circle, especially in meg og mine (“me and my loved ones”). Substantivized neuter mitt can refer collectively to the speaker's possessions, interests, or affairs.

              Etymology 2

              Norwegian Wikipedia has an article on:
              Minutt
              Wikipedia no

              Clipping of minutt (“minute”), also used as a written abbreviation. The full form derives from Latin minūta (“small; diminished”), in pars minuta prima (“first small part”), from Latin minuō (“make smaller”), from Proto-Italic *minuō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“small; little”).

              Compare the parallel clipping English min (“minute”).

              Pronunciation

              • (spoken clipping) IPA(key): /mɪnː/, [mɪnː]
              • Rhymes: -ɪnː
              • Homophone: minn
              • Hyphenation: min

              Noun

              min n (indefinite plural min)

              1. (colloquial) clipping of minutt (“minute”).
                Jeg kommer om fem min. ― I'll be there in five minutes.
                • 2017 March 11, Ingvill Dybfest Dahl, “«Mesternes mester»-Anders Jacobsen: – Det må investeres i kjærestetid”, in VG‎:
                  det tar bare ti min, så er du i Nordmarka
                  It only takes ten minutes, and then you're in Nordmarka.
                • 2023, Oliver Lovrenski, Da vi var yngre, page 110:
                  etter fem–ti min vi var ute [av butikken] igjen
                  After five to ten minutes we were outside [the shop] again.
              2. abbreviation of minutt (“minute”).[1]
                Steketid: 20 min. ― Cooking time: 20 min.
              Usage notes
              • The spoken clipping is used only in indefinite singular and plural, both min.
              • The written abbreviation has no full stop and may be read in full as minutt or minutter. The pronunciation above represents the spoken clipping.

              Etymology 3

              Clipping of minus (“minus”), from Latin minus (“less”), the neuter form of minor (“smaller; less”), from Proto-Italic *minōs (“less”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“small; little”).

              Pronunciation

              • IPA(key): /miːn/, [miːn]
              • Rhymes: -iːn
              • Hyphenation: min

              Adverb

              min

              1. (colloquial, education) minus; following a school grade, indicating performance slightly below that grade.
                Jeg fikk fire min på prøven. ― I got a four minus on the test.
                • 1992, Lars Saabye Christensen, Ingens, page 53:
                  hvis du klarer alle stykkene, får’u nuggen min
                  If you solve all the problems, you'll get a “nuggen” minus [a school grade].

                  Portuguese

                  Pronunciation

                  • (Brazil) IPA(key): /ˈmĩ/
                  • (Portugal) IPA(key): /ˈmin/

                  • Hyphenation: min

                  Etymology 1

                  Noun

                  min m (invariable)

                  1. abbreviation of minuto
                    1. Used to indicate time in relation to an hour on a 24-hour clock.
                      O evento é hoje, às 20h30min ― The event is today at 8:30 p.m.
                    2. Used to indicate any sequence of time in minutes.
                      O atleta completou a corrida em 1h20min45s ― The athlete completed the race in 1 hour, 21 minutes and 45 seconds
                  Usage notes
                  • This abbreviation uses no spaces or points and must always follow a number (in its most common usage, a number between 00 and 59 to indicate the minutes of an hour).
                  • This abbreviation is often preceded by a number followed by h, used to represent hours.
                  • The abbreviation can be followed by another abbreviation, s, to represent seconds.
                    • Example: 20h43min08s

                  1. Min

                  Welsh

                  Etymology

                  According to Stokes, from Proto-Celtic *maknā, *meknos, from Proto-Indo-European *mak-, *maks- (“bag, bellows, belly”), see also English maw.[1]

                  Pronunciation

                  • IPA(key): /miːn/
                  • Rhymes: -iːn

                  Noun

                  min m (plural minion)

                  1. point, sharp edge
                    Synonyms: ymyl, awch
                  2. edge, border, brim
                    Synonyms: ymyl, ochr, byl
                  3. lip
                    Synonym: gwefus
